title: AI Benefits at Work Unevenly Distributed
key_facts: Gallup surveyed 7,845 US employees who use AI at work (fielded 26 Jan to 24 Mar 2026): 63% say AI helps them work faster and 56% say it helps them find more creative solutions.
47% say AI lets them spend more time on the most interesting parts of their job and 46% say it helps them produce higher-quality work.
31% of AI users say their AI use led their employer to ask them to take on more responsibilities (37% among those who say AI makes them faster; 38% among users aged 18 to 24).

28% of all employees use AI at least weekly and 54% say they have not used it in their role; healthcare support, manufacturing production and retail sales workers mostly never use it (70% to more than 80%).
College graduates are more than twice as likely as non-graduates to use AI daily or weekly (40% vs 17%); 37% of managers versus 25% of individual contributors are regular users.

Among AI users, 68% of four-year graduates say AI helps them work faster versus 51% of those with a high school education or less; about seven in ten of the highest paid (USD 10,000 or more a month) say the same versus 58% of those earning under USD 4,000.
52% of weekly AI users have a quality job versus 32% of workers who never use AI, but Gallup says more research is needed because the same groups tend both to hold quality jobs and to use AI more.

The findings are workers' own assessments, not employers'; they are the first results of year two of the American Job Quality Study (Jobs for the Future, The Families & Workers Fund and Gallup), with the full report due in late October 2026.
quote_evidence: These findings are based on employees’ own assessments of how AI is affecting their work and do not establish whether employers would evaluate its effects in the same way.
College graduates are more than twice as likely as those without a college degree to say they use AI on a daily or weekly basis (40% vs. 17%, respectively).
Majorities of U.S. employees who have used AI in their job say it helps them do their job faster (63%) and find more creative solutions to work tasks (56%).
why_it_matters_hint: AI's workplace benefits are reaching better-educated, higher-paid and managerial workers first, so the gap between workers could widen.
event_date: Gallup release dated 5 Oct 2026 (survey fielded 26 Jan to 24 Mar 2026).
notes: Read in full. Gallup's own release (primary source), hence CONFIRMED for the existence and method of the survey; the results themselves are self-reported by workers. Margins of sampling error: plus or minus 1 point (all employees, n=15,482) and plus or minus 2 points (AI users, n=7,845).
